paper_metadata.title: Longitudinal Functional Connectome in Pediatric Concussion: An Advancing Concussion Assessment in Pediatrics Study

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study utilizes a large, multi-site prospective cohort (A-CAP) with clearly defined inclusion/exclusion criteria for both concussion and a robust orthopedic injury (OI) control group. While there is some evidence of selection bias in the MRI sub-sample (younger and more male), the overall representation of the target population is high.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Study recruitment occurred in the emergency department of five children's hospitals that are all members of the Pediatric Emergency Research Canada (PERC) network
items.reasoning: The source population is clearly defined as children presenting to pediatric emergency departments across multiple Canadian sites.

items.evidence_snippet: A total of 6449 children were screened in the ED, 3051 were eligible, and 979 were consented and enrolled
items.reasoning: The recruitment flow is transparently reported, showing a systematic screening process in the ED.

items.evidence_snippet: Alberta Children's Hospital (Calgary), Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario (Ottawa), Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Sainte-Justine (Montreal), Stollery Children's Hospital (Edmonton), and British Columbia Children's Hospital (Vancouver).

items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: consistent with the World Health Organization definition of mild TBI: (1) observed loss of consciousness, (2) Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13–14, or (3) at least one acute sign or symptom of concussion
items.reasoning: Criteria are based on established WHO definitions and specific clinical parameters.

items.evidence_snippet: of 3075 eligible children, 967 consented to participate
items.reasoning: The participation rate is approximately 31%, which is common for neuroimaging studies but lower than the ideal 80% threshold for low risk.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Attrition rates are significant (up to 28% at 6 months). While the authors analyzed differences between returners and non-returners, finding only parental education differences at 6 months, the loss of nearly 30% of the sample introduces potential for informative censoring.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: Overall study attrition rates were 15%, 25%, and 28% for the post-acute, 3-month, and 6-month assessments, respectively
items.reasoning: Attrition is within expected ranges for longitudinal TBI research but exceeds 20%, which warrants caution.

items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: Orthodontia and scheduling difficulties were the most common reasons that MRI was not completed.
items.reasoning: Reasons for missing MRI scans are provided, but specific reasons for general study attrition (the 28%) are not detailed.

items.reasoning: The authors explicitly compared characteristics of those lost to follow-up versus those who remained.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The primary prognostic factor (concussion vs. OI) is well-defined. The secondary factor (symptom persistence) uses a validated tool (HBI) and a statistically rigorous Reliable Change Index (RCI) to categorize participants.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: A reliable change index z-score comparing total 1-month post-injury symptom scores to pre-morbid scores was calculated
items.reasoning: The definition of persistent symptoms is mathematically defined using RCI.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: The Health and Behavior Inventory was used to assess cognitive and somatic symptoms. This measure has good internal consistency and test–retest reliability
items.reasoning: The HBI is a validated instrument in pediatric TBI research.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: classify children with concussion into two groups using a critical z-score >1.65 (one-tailed p<0.05)
items.reasoning: The cut-point for symptom persistence is based on standard statistical thresholds (z > 1.65).

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Total pre-morbid (pre-injury) symptoms were rated by parents during the post-acute visit, and total post-injury symptoms were rated by both parents and children weekly
items.reasoning: Standardized timing and methods were used for all participants.

items.evidence_snippet: Of the children who completed MRI, 661 completed at least one resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) scan
items.reasoning: A high proportion of the MRI-eligible sample provided usable data.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: PF Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: PF is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcome (functional connectome) was measured using advanced rs-fMRI with rigorous quality control, denoising, and harmonization across sites. The use of graph theory metrics is a standard, objective approach.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: Graph theory metrics were derived from 918 resting-state functional MRI scans... Global and regional (nodal) level metrics included clustering coefficient, small-worldness, efficiency, betweenness centrality, and degree centrality.
items.reasoning: Outcomes are clearly defined as specific graph theory metrics.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Each functional run was denoised using AFNI's 3dTproject... network metrics were harmonized for site (scanner) differences using ComBAT
items.reasoning: Extensive technical steps (denoising, motion correction, ComBAT harmonization) were taken to ensure measurement reliability.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: At all sites, children were asked to keep their eyes open, not think of anything, and look at a cross presented on a screen.
items.reasoning: The rs-fMRI protocol was standardized across all five sites.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Outcome Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Outcome of interest is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study design uses an OI control group to control for general injury factors. The statistical analysis uses linear mixed-effects models that adjust for age, sex, and site (via ComBAT), which are the primary confounders in this population.
